pages.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his guardians due to early growth concern. They noticed pubic hair development last month and an unusual growth spurt recently. The child has no reported changes in appetite or energy levels and excels academically. There is no family history of genetic syndromes or endocrine disorders. On examination, mild pubic hair (Tanner stage 2) and enlarged testicular volume (Tanner stage 3) are noted. Genital examination shows no abnormalities. His bone age is significantly advanced by two years. An ultrasound of the testes is normal. Serum levels of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicular stimulating hormone (FSH) are elevated. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals no masses or abnormalities. What is the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?

answers.text: Pituitary adenoma producing human chorionic gonadotropin
Early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis

pages.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his guardians due to early growth concern. They noticed pubic hair development last month and an unusual growth spurt recently. The child has no reported changes in appetite or energy levels and excels academically. There is no family history of genetic syndromes or endocrine disorders. On examination, mild pubic hair (Tanner stage 2) and enlarged testicular volume (Tanner stage 3) are noted. Genital examination shows no abnormalities. His bone age is significantly advanced by two years. An ultrasound of the testes is normal. Serum levels of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicular stimulating hormone (FSH) are elevated. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals no masses or abnormalities. What is the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?

answers.text:
Pituitary adenoma producing human chorionic gonadotropin
(9.77%)

Early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
(70.68%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The elevated FSH and LH levels indicate central precocious puberty due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, causing early onset of secondary sexual characteristics and advanced bone age. The normal imaging studies rule out structural causes, making idiopathic central precocious puberty the most likely diagnosis.
(Choice A)
Pituitary adenoma producing human chorionic gonadotropin
Pituitary adenomas rarely produce hCG. Gonadotropin-producing pituitary adenomas would actually cause elevated LH and FSH, making this a less likely but possible cause that would require MRI brain imaging to exclude.
(Choice B)
Gonadotropin-secreting germ cell tumor
Gonadotropin-secreting germ cell tumors can cause precocious puberty with elevated LH and FSH, similar to central precocious puberty. However, the normal testicular ultrasound and abdominal CT make this less likely in this case.
(Choice C)
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically results in peripheral precocious puberty with suppressed LH and FSH due to excess adrenal androgen production causing negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
(Choice D)
Early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
This condition causes central precocious puberty, as seen here with elevated FSH and LH due to premature activation of the HPG axis.
(Choice E)
Adrenal gland tumor secreting testosterone
An adrenal tumor secreting testosterone causes peripheral precocious puberty with suppressed LH and FSH levels due to negative feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

pages.question: A 68-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to his primary care physician for a routine follow-up. He has been using inhaled beclomethasone twice daily for the past six months to manage his symptoms. During the visit, he mentions noticing some white patches on his tongue and inside his cheeks, along with mild discomfort while swallowing. He denies fever, cough, or changes in his respiratory symptoms. Physical examination reveals adherent white plaques on the oral mucosa that can be scraped off, leaving a red base. What is the most common adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroid therapy that this patient is likely experiencing?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The most common adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroid therapy is oropharyngeal thrush (oral candidiasis), which occurs due to local immunosuppression in the mouth and throat. This can be prevented by using a spacer device and rinsing the mouth after inhaler use. Systemic effects like adrenal suppression, cataracts, and osteoporosis can occur with high-dose inhaled steroids (typically >800 mcg/day beclomethasone equivalent) but are less common than local effects.
(Choice A)
Oral candidiasis
Oral candidiasis (thrush) is the most common adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroid therapy due to local deposition of the steroid in the oropharynx, which promotes fungal overgrowth.
(Choice B)
Hoarseness
Hoarseness (dysphonia) can occur due to local effects on the vocal cords from inhaled corticosteroids, but it is less common than oral candidiasis.
(Choice C)
Adrenal suppression
Adrenal suppression can occur with inhaled corticosteroids, particularly at high doses (>800 mcg/day beclomethasone equivalent), but this patient's symptoms are clearly localized to the oropharynx rather than systemic.
(Choice D)
Cataract formation
While cataract formation can occur with prolonged high-dose inhaled corticosteroids, this patient's acute presentation with visible oral lesions points to the more common local adverse effect of oral candidiasis.
(Choice E)
Skin purpura
Skin purpura and easy bruising can occur with high-dose inhaled corticosteroids due to dermal thinning, but this patient's symptoms are localized to the oral cavity, making oral candidiasis the more likely diagnosis.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents to the emergency department with fatigue, abdominal distension, and leg swelling that has worsened over the past three weeks. He reports no fever, chills, or abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals jaundice, spider angiomata, and moderate ascites with shifting dullness. Laboratory studies are shown below. Abdominal ultrasound confirms ascites and nodular liver contour suggestive of cirrhosis. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed. Which of the following tests on the ascitic fluid is most essential to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?



Hemoglobin	13.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	39%
White blood cell count	8200 /mm³
Platelet count	160000 /μL
Mean corpuscular volume	88 fL
Sodium	138 mEq/L
Potassium	4.0 mEq/L
Chloride	102 mEq/L
Bicarbonate	24 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen	18 mg/dL
Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Glucose	95 mg/dL
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)	180 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)	200 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase	220 U/L
Total bilirubin	2.8 mg/dL
Albumin	2.5 g/dL
Prothrombin time	18 seconds
INR	1.6
pages.explanation:
Explanation
In patients with new-onset ascites, diagnostic paracentesis is required. The most essential test is ascitic fluid cell count and differential to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), defined by neutrophil count ≥250/mm³. Additional routine tests include total protein and serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) to determine etiology. Other specialized tests like cytology, amylase, or triglycerides are indicated only when specific conditions are suspected based on clinical presentation.
(Choice A)
Gram stain and culture
While Gram stain and culture are important tests for ascitic fluid, they are secondary to cell count and differential. The cell count with neutrophil count ≥250/mm³ is the primary diagnostic criterion for SBP and determines the need for empirical antibiotic therapy. Gram stain is positive in only 10-20% of SBP cases, and culture results take 24-48 hours, making them less useful for immediate clinical decision-making.
(Choice B)
Cell count and differential
Cell count and differential are essential in all diagnostic paracenteses for new-onset ascites to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, as a neutrophil count ≥250/mm³ indicates infection requiring prompt treatment.
(Choice C)
Lactate dehydrogenase level
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level can help differentiate between spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and secondary bacterial peritonitis, as very high LDH levels (>upper limit of normal for serum) suggest secondary peritonitis. However, it is not essential for ruling out SBP itself, which is diagnosed primarily by neutrophil count ≥250/mm³.
(Choice D)
Triglyceride level
Triglyceride level is measured to assess for chylous ascites, typically in cases of lymphatic obstruction, but it is not a routine test for all new-onset ascites.
(Choice E)
Amylase level
Amylase level is used to evaluate for pancreatic ascites, which is not routinely indicated in all cases of new-onset ascites unless there is suspicion of pancreatic disease.

pages.question: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic by her foster parents for evaluation of behavioral concerns. They report that she has difficulty staying seated during meals, often interrupts others during conversations, and struggles to complete her chores without constant reminders. These behaviors have been ongoing for the past year and are causing strain in the household. The girl is in fourth grade and her foster parents have not yet discussed her school performance with her teachers, but they note she brings home average grades. She has no history of trauma, seizures, or sensory deficits, and her physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This girl presents with symptoms suggestive of ADHD, including inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity at home for over one year, causing functional impairment. DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ADHD require evidence of symptoms and impairment in at least two settings (typically home and school), making teacher evaluations essential to assess school behavior and academic functioning. Stimulant therapy should not be initiated without a confirmed diagnosis through comprehensive evaluation. Routine neuroimaging, laboratory tests, or sensory screening are not indicated without specific clinical concerns. Reassurance alone without proper evaluation may miss important functional impacts on the child's development and academic performance.
(Choice A)
Initiate methylphenidate therapy
Stimulant medication should not be initiated without first establishing a confirmed diagnosis of ADHD through comprehensive evaluation. DSM-5 criteria require evidence of symptoms and functional impairment in at least two settings (home and school) before diagnosis can be made.
(Choice B)
Obtain teacher evaluations
Teacher input is crucial to confirm symptoms and impairment in the school setting, fulfilling diagnostic criteria for ADHD.
(Choice C)
Perform thyroid function tests
Thyroid testing is not necessary unless there are symptoms suggestive of thyroid dysfunction, which are absent here.
(Choice D)
Conduct vision and hearing screening
Vision and hearing screening are important components of general pediatric care, but are not the priority when evaluating suspected ADHD. The child's average academic performance and lack of reported academic concerns make sensory deficits less likely as the primary cause of her behavioral symptoms.
(Choice E)
Order brain magnetic resonance imaging
Neuroimaging is not routinely indicated for ADHD diagnosis unless there are signs of neurological abnormalities.

pages.question:
A 32-year-old female at 9 weeks of gestation comes to the clinic with complaints of persistent nausea, vomiting, and noticeable weight loss. She has difficulty keeping down water and has been vomiting multiple times a day for the past few weeks. On examination, she appears dehydrated. Vital signs reveal a heart rate of 110 beats per minute and blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory tests show:

Urinalysis:
- Protein: negative
- Blood: negative
- Glucose: negative
- Ketones: positive
- White blood cells: 1-2/hpf

Liver Function Tests:
- Total bilirubin: 1.2 mg/dL
- AST: 110 U/L
- ALT: 180 U/L
- Alkaline phosphatase: 135 U/L
- Amylase: 180 U/L
- Lipase: 115 U/L

Based on the findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed when persistent vomiting leads to significant dehydration and notable metabolic changes, such as ketonuria. Elevated liver enzymes can be seen with the stress of vomiting. The diagnosis is primarily a clinical one differentiating from milder forms of pregnancy-related nausea.
(Choice A)
Gallstone pancreatitis
While gallstone pancreatitis can occur in pregnancy and cause nausea/vomiting, it typically presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, and lipase levels are usually markedly elevated (>3x upper limit of normal). The modest elevation here and absence of characteristic pain make this less likely.
(Choice B)
Hyperemesis gravidarum
Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed with persistent vomiting, >5% weight loss, and ketonuria during early pregnancy. Elevated liver enzymes and metabolic disturbances support this diagnosis.
(Choice C)
Biliary colic
Biliary colic presents with episodic right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often postprandial, without persistent vomiting or ketonuria. Liver enzymes are typically normal unless there is associated cholangitis or choledocholithiasis.
(Choice D)
Viral gastroenteritis
Gastroenteritis typically features diarrhea, which is not present in this case. Elevated AST, ALT, and ketonuria are atypical for gastroenteritis.
(Choice E)
Preeclampsia
Preeclampsia typically occurs after 20 weeks gestation and is characterized by new-onset hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) with proteinuria or other end-organ damage. This patient is at 9 weeks with hypotension, not hypertension, and has negative proteinuria.

pages.question:
A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after falling from a height while rock climbing. She reports severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and shortness of breath. On examination, she  has a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg, a heart rate of 120 beats/min, and has tenderness over the right lower chest and upper abdomen. A Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) exam reveals free fluid in the hepatorenal recess and pelvis. Her lab values and examination of right flank area are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?



Hemoglobin	9.5 g/dL
RBC	3.5 ×10^12/L
Hematocrit	29 %
MCV	83 fL
MCH	27 pg
MCHC	32 g/dL
Platelets	250 ×10^9/L
WBC	6.5 ×10^9/L
Neutrophils	55 %
Lymphocytes	35 %
Monocytes	7 %
Eosinophils	2 %
Basophils	1 %
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Blunt abdominal trauma from a fall with right upper quadrant pain, hypotension, tachycardia, right flank ecchymoses, and free intraperitoneal fluid on FAST is most consistent with liver laceration causing intraabdominal hemorrhage. Abdominal aortic rupture is uncommon in blunt trauma and typically fatal prehospital. Splenic hematoma often contains bleeding without significant free fluid. Pancreatic injury is usually retroperitoneal and does not cause free intraperitoneal fluid. Duodenal perforation may lead to retroperitoneal air but not typically massive free fluid with shock. Urinary bladder rupture can cause free fluid but hemodynamic instability is less severe unless associated with other injuries.
(Choice A)
Pancreatic transection
Pancreatic transection is retroperitoneal and would not typically cause the significant free intraperitoneal fluid seen on FAST exam. It more commonly presents with epigastric pain, elevated lipase, and may show retroperitoneal fluid collections on CT.
(Choice B)
Splenic laceration
Splenic laceration would typically present with left upper quadrant pain and left flank ecchymoses (Kehr sign), not right-sided findings as described in this case.
(Choice C)
Duodenal perforation
Duodenal injuries often result in retroperitoneal air or fluid but not massive free intraperitoneal hemorrhage leading to shock.
(Choice D)
Liver laceration
The clinical presentation of blunt trauma with hypotension, right upper quadrant pain, flank ecchymoses, anemia, and free fluid on FAST strongly suggests liver laceration with intraabdominal bleeding, a common injury in such scenarios.
(Choice E)
Abdominal aortic rupture
Abdominal aortic rupture is rare in blunt trauma and often leads to immediate exsanguination and death before reaching the hospital.

pages.question:
A 55-year-old woman who works in a chemical factory with known exposure to benzene presents to the clinic with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue, recurrent upper respiratory infections, and frequent nosebleeds. She also reports easy bruising after minor trauma. Physical examination reveals pallor, scattered petechiae on her lower extremities, and no splenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. A bone marrow biopsy is performed. What is the most likely mechanism underlying this patient's thrombocytopenia?



Hemoglobin	7.2 g/dL
RBC	2.2 ×10^12/L
Hematocrit	21 %
MCV	92 fL
MCH	33 pg
MCHC	32 g/dL
Platelets	25 ×10^9/L
WBC	2.1 ×10^9/L
Neutrophils	55 %
Lymphocytes	35 %
Monocytes	7 %
Eosinophils	2 %
Basophils	1 %
Prothrombin Time (PT) 12	(range: 11–13.5 seconds)
Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT / aPTT) 32	(range: 25–35 seconds)
Peripheral Smear	Pancytopenia, morphology normal, no blasts or dysplasia
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient presents with pancytopenia (low RBC, WBC, and platelets) with normal cell morphology on peripheral smear and normal coagulation studies. The combination of chronic symptoms (fatigue, infections, bleeding), benzene exposure, and pancytopenia is classic for aplastic anemia. In aplastic anemia, bone marrow failure results from damage to hematopoietic stem cells, leading to decreased production of all cell lines including megakaryocytes, which causes thrombocytopenia through reduced platelet production.
(Choice A)
Defective platelet function
Defective platelet function occurs in inherited disorders like Glanzmann thrombasthenia or acquired conditions affecting platelet aggregation. These disorders cause bleeding due to poor platelet function despite normal platelet counts, which contradicts this patient's severe thrombocytopenia and pancytopenia.
(Choice B)
Decreased megakaryocyte production
In aplastic anemia, bone marrow failure leads to reduced production of all hematopoietic cell lines, including megakaryocytes, resulting in thrombocytopenia.
(Choice C)
Increased peripheral platelet destruction
This mechanism occurs in conditions like immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). However, these conditions typically present with isolated thrombocytopenia and normal or hypercellular bone marrow, not the pancytopenia and hypocellular marrow seen in this patient.
(Choice D)
Platelet sequestration in the spleen
Hypersplenism causes thrombocytopenia through platelet sequestration in an enlarged spleen. This patient has no splenomegaly on examination, and hypersplenism would not explain the concurrent anemia and leukopenia (pancytopenia) seen here.
(Choice E)
Dilutional thrombocytopenia from massive transfusion
Dilutional thrombocytopenia occurs when massive transfusion of packed red blood cells dilutes the patient's platelet count. This patient has no transfusion history and presents with chronic progressive symptoms over 2 months, making acute dilutional effects impossible.

pages.question:
A 76-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of increasing fatigue and shortness of breath for the past two months. He reports no significant medical history and is not on any medications. His vital signs reveal a temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure of 145/88 mm Hg, heart rate of 110/min, and respiratory rate of 22/min. On physical examination, there is a soft, grade 2/6 ejection murmur at the right sternal border. His extremities are free of edema, and stool tests for occult blood return negative results. Basic lab work shows: 
Hemoglobin: 9.0 g/dL 
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV): 75 fl 
Platelet count: 370,000/mm3 
Leukocyte count: 5,000/mm3 
Neutrophils: 58% 
Eosinophils: 2% 
Lymphocytes: 32% 
Monocytes: 8% 



Serum ferritin: 6 ng/mL
Serum iron: 38 µg/dL
Total iron-binding capacity: 420 µg/dL

What is the most appropriate investigation to perform next on this patient?

answers.text:
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This elderly male presents with iron deficiency anemia (low hemoglobin, low MCV, low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC). In elderly patients with iron deficiency anemia, occult gastrointestinal bleeding is the most common cause and must be investigated even when fecal occult blood tests are negative. Colonoscopy is the initial procedure of choice in this population due to the high prevalence of colonic sources (polyps, malignancy) and superior diagnostic yield compared to upper endoscopy as the first procedure.
(Choice A)
Colonoscopy
Iron studies confirm iron deficiency anemia. In an elderly male with confirmed IDA and no identified bleeding source, colonoscopy is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for occult lower gastrointestinal blood loss from colonic polyps or malignancy — even in the setting of a negative FOBT, which has limited sensitivity.
(Choice B)
Upper GI endoscopy
While upper GI endoscopy (EGD) is important in the workup of iron deficiency anemia, current guidelines recommend colonoscopy as the initial procedure in elderly patients due to the higher yield of significant pathology in the colon. EGD would typically be performed if colonoscopy is negative or if there are upper GI symptoms.
(Choice C)
Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is not the appropriate initial investigation for iron deficiency anemia. While it could detect hepatosplenomegaly or abdominal masses, it would not identify the most common sources of occult GI bleeding in elderly patients (colonic polyps or malignancy) that cause iron deficiency anemia.
(Choice D)
Repeat stool occult test
Repeating stool occult blood testing is not appropriate as the next step. Fecal occult blood tests have poor sensitivity (especially single tests) and can miss significant lesions. Given the established iron deficiency anemia in an elderly male, direct visualization with colonoscopy is indicated regardless of FOBT results.
(Choice E)
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is not the appropriate initial investigation for iron deficiency anemia. While CT can detect masses, it has limited ability to identify mucosal lesions, small polyps, or early malignancies that commonly cause occult GI bleeding. Direct endoscopic evaluation is the standard of care.

pages.question: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily presents for a follow-up visit. His HbA1c is 7.6%, up from 7.2% three months ago. He denies missed medication doses. A dietary review reveals that he has recently started drinking two 12-ounce servings of fruit juice daily, believing that because juice comes from fruit it is a healthy carbohydrate choice equivalent to eating whole fruit. His fasting glucose today is 148 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains the glycemic difference between consuming whole fruit versus fruit juice?

answers.text:
Whole fruit contains added sugars from processing, which have a higher glycemic index than natural fruit sugars
(0%)

Whole fruit retains dietary fiber that slows gastric emptying and glucose absorption, while juicing removes the fiber matrix, resulting in rapid glucose delivery and higher postprandial glucose excursions
(85.71%)

Fruit juice contains higher concentrations of fructose per serving than whole fruit, and fructose is directly converted to glucose in the liver
(14.29%)

The vitamins in whole fruit inhibit intestinal glucose transporters, reducing glucose absorption compared to juice
(0%)

Fruit juice is absorbed more slowly because its liquid form dilutes gastric enzymes and slows carbohydrate digestion
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Whole fruit contains intact dietary fiber that slows gastric emptying and reduces the rate of glucose absorption, resulting in a lower glycemic index compared to fruit juice. Fruit juice removes most of the fiber matrix, causing rapid glucose delivery to the small intestine and greater postprandial glucose excursions, which is clinically relevant in patients with type 2 diabetes.
(Choice A)
Whole fruit contains added sugars from processing, which have a higher glycemic index than natural fruit sugars
This answer incorrectly reverses the relationship between whole fruit and added sugars. Whole, unprocessed fruit contains only naturally occurring sugars (glucose, fructose, and sucrose). It is processed fruit products and many commercial fruit juices that may contain added sugars like high fructose corn syrup or sucrose. Additionally, the glycemic difference between whole fruit and juice is primarily due to fiber content, not the type of sugars present. This choice is incorrect because it mischaracterizes both the sugar content and the underlying physiological mechanism.
(Choice B)
Whole fruit retains dietary fiber that slows gastric emptying and glucose absorption, while juicing removes the fiber matrix, resulting in rapid glucose delivery and higher postprandial glucose excursions
The intact cellular and fiber structure of whole fruit, including both soluble and insoluble fiber, creates a physical barrier that slows gastric emptying and reduces the rate of carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption in the small intestine. When fruit is juiced, the majority of this fiber matrix is removed, allowing the natural sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose) to be rapidly absorbed, producing a sharply elevated postprandial glucose response. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that consumption of whole fruit is associated with reduced risk of type 2 diabetes, whereas fruit juice consumption is associated with increased risk, underscoring the glycemic importance of fiber preservation. The glycemic index of whole oranges, for example, is approximately 40 to 45, whereas orange juice ranges from 50 to 65, reflecting this physiological difference. For patients with type 2 diabetes, replacing fruit juice with whole fruit and encouraging adequate dietary fiber intake is a key dietary counseling strategy to improve glycemic control.
(Choice C)
Fruit juice contains higher concentrations of fructose per serving than whole fruit, and fructose is directly converted to glucose in the liver
While fructose is metabolized primarily in the liver and can contribute to hepatic glucose production via gluconeogenesis, this answer incorrectly identifies fructose content as the primary differentiator. Whole fruit and equivalent amounts of fruit juice contain similar fructose concentrations. The key glycemic difference stems from fiber removal during juicing, not inherent differences in fructose metabolism. The fiber matrix in whole fruit creates physical barriers that slow gastric emptying and glucose absorption, effects that are lost when fruit is processed into juice.
(Choice D)
The vitamins in whole fruit inhibit intestinal glucose transporters, reducing glucose absorption compared to juice
There is no established mechanism by which vitamins in whole fruit meaningfully inhibit intestinal glucose transporters (such as SGLT1 or GLUT5) to a clinically significant degree. The primary determinant of the glycemic difference between whole fruit and juice is the presence or absence of dietary fiber, not vitamin content. This distractor incorrectly attributes the glycemic benefit of whole fruit to its micronutrient content.
(Choice E)
Fruit juice is absorbed more slowly because its liquid form dilutes gastric enzymes and slows carbohydrate digestion
This reasoning is physiologically incorrect. Liquids generally accelerate gastric emptying compared to solid foods, which means fruit juice is absorbed more rapidly, not more slowly, than whole fruit. The liquid form of juice removes the mechanical and fiber-related barriers to rapid glucose absorption, worsening postprandial glycemic excursions rather than attenuating them.

pages.question: A 22-year-old male college wrestler presents to the clinic with multiple small, asymptomatic skin lesions on his upper arms and trunk that developed over the past two weeks following a wrestling tournament. He reports close skin-to-skin contact with opponents during matches. Physical examination reveals lesions seen in the picture below. The lesions are nontender, and there is no surrounding erythema. The patient is otherwise healthy with no history of immunosuppression or recent sexual activity. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient's condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with molluscum contagiosum, a benign poxvirus infection acquired through skin-to-skin contact, common in contact sports like wrestling. The characteristic small, firm papules with central umbilication allow for clinical diagnosis without need for biopsy. First-line therapy in adults includes cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, curettage, or topical agents like cantharidin. Given the isolated, non-genital lesions and lack of extensive disease, STI screening is not indicated. Antiviral therapies like acyclovir are ineffective against poxviruses, topical corticosteroids may worsen the condition, and antibiotics are not appropriate for viral infections.
(Choice A)
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen is a first-line treatment for molluscum contagiosum in adults, effectively destroying the lesions with minimal scarring.
(Choice B)
Punch biopsy and histopathologic examination
Diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum is typically clinical based on characteristic appearance; biopsy is unnecessary unless the diagnosis is uncertain.
(Choice C)
Topical hydrocortisone
Topical corticosteroids can suppress local immune responses, potentially allowing viral proliferation and increasing lesion count or duration. They may also predispose to secondary bacterial infection of the lesions.
(Choice D)
Oral cephalexin
Oral antibiotics like cephalexin target bacterial infections and have no efficacy against viral pathogens such as the poxvirus causing molluscum contagiosum. Antibiotics would not address the underlying viral etiology.
(Choice E)
Topical acyclovir
Topical acyclovir is effective against herpes simplex virus, which is a DNA virus from the Herpesviridae family. Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus, making antiviral therapy ineffective.

pages.question: A 42-year-old professional violinist presents with a 4-month history of intermittent tremor in his left hand. He reports that the tremor is most prominent when he is at rest, such as when watching television, and it significantly diminishes when he is actively playing his violin or performing other purposeful movements. On examination, the tremor has a frequency of approximately 6 Hz, is asymmetric, and is accompanied by mild cogwheel rigidity in the left arm. There is no bradykinesia or postural instability noted. His medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no medications. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment for this patient's condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with early-stage Parkinson disease (PD), characterized by an asymmetric resting tremor that improves with voluntary movement and is associated with rigidity. While trihexyphenidyl can be used for tremor-predominant PD in younger patients, current evidence-based guidelines recommend levodopa/carbidopa or dopamine agonists as first-line therapy. Anticholinergics are typically reserved as adjunctive treatment due to potential cognitive side effects.
(Choice A)
Trihexyphenidyl
While trihexyphenidyl can be effective for tremor-dominant Parkinson disease in younger patients, current guidelines recommend levodopa/carbidopa or dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) as first-line therapy. Anticholinergics are typically reserved as adjunctive therapy due to potential cognitive side effects, even in younger patients.
(Choice B)
Clonazepam
Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine that may be used as adjunctive therapy for various movement disorders but is not a first-line treatment for Parkinson disease. The primary concern is that it does not address the underlying dopaminergic dysfunction in PD.
(Choice C)
Propranolol
Propranolol is a beta-blocker that is first-line therapy for essential tremor, which typically occurs during action or posture maintenance. This patient has a resting tremor that improves with voluntary movement, which is characteristic of Parkinson disease, not essential tremor.
(Choice D)
Clozapine
Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic that can actually worsen Parkinson disease symptoms due to its dopamine receptor blocking properties. It has no role in treating PD tremor and would be contraindicated in this patient.
(Choice E)
Primidone
Primidone is an anticonvulsant that serves as first-line therapy for essential tremor, which is an action tremor that occurs during voluntary movement. This patient's resting tremor that improves with movement is characteristic of Parkinson disease, making primidone inappropriate.

pages.question: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (stage 3) is evaluated postoperatively following elective hip replacement surgery. Her wound shows dehiscence on postoperative day 10, with poor granulation tissue and surrounding erythema. She has been on a renal diet limiting protein intake to 0.6 g/kg/day for the past 2 years. Laboratory studies show albumin 2.6 g/dL, prealbumin 10 mg/dL, zinc 52 mcg/dL (normal: 60–130 mcg/dL), and a mildly elevated creatinine. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for the impaired wound healing in this patient?

answers.text:
Hyperglycemia-induced reactive oxygen species damaging wound bed vasculature
(0%)

Protein malnutrition reducing amino acid availability for collagen synthesis
(50%)

Vitamin C deficiency impairing hydroxylation of procollagen during collagen synthesis
(0%)

Zinc deficiency impairing fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
(50%)

Vitamin A deficiency impairing epithelialization and keratinocyte differentiation
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Zinc is an essential cofactor for RNA and DNA polymerases, metalloproteinases, and over 300 enzymes involved in cell proliferation and protein synthesis. Deficiency impairs fibroblast replication, collagen synthesis, and neutrophil chemotaxis, all critical for wound healing. Zinc deficiency is common in patients with chronic kidney disease due to reduced dietary intake, impaired intestinal absorption, and increased urinary losses.
(Choice A)
Hyperglycemia-induced reactive oxygen species damaging wound bed vasculature
Hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus does contribute to impaired wound healing through multiple mechanisms, including increased oxidative stress, reduced growth factor signaling, impaired neutrophil function, and microvascular disease leading to tissue hypoxia. While diabetes is relevant context in this patient, the question specifically asks for the mechanism best supported by the laboratory findings provided. The documented low serum zinc level (52 mcg/dL) identifies a specific, correctable nutritional deficiency that directly accounts for the impaired fibroblast activity and poor granulation tissue observed.
(Choice B)
Protein malnutrition reducing amino acid availability for collagen synthesis
Protein malnutrition is a significant contributing factor in this patient — her albumin of 2.6 g/dL and prealbumin of 10 mg/dL reflect poor visceral protein stores, and her protein-restricted diet (0.6 g/kg/day) limits amino acid substrate needed for collagen synthesis and immune function. However, the question asks for the mechanism best supported by the laboratory data provided, and the documented low serum zinc level (52 mcg/dL) identifies a specific, measurable micronutrient deficiency that directly impairs fibroblast proliferation and metalloproteinase activity essential for wound healing.
(Choice C)
Vitamin C deficiency impairing hydroxylation of procollagen during collagen synthesis
Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen cross-linking by reducing prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase activity, and would certainly impair wound healing. However, this patient has no clinical features of scurvy (no perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, or bleeding gums), and no serum ascorbate level is reported as low. The laboratory findings specifically document zinc deficiency, making that the best-supported mechanistic explanation for the wound dehiscence in this clinical scenario.
(Choice D)
Zinc deficiency impairing fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
Zinc is a critical micronutrient required for the activity of over 300 metalloenzymes, including RNA and DNA polymerases, alkaline phosphatase, and matrix metalloproteinases, all of which are essential for normal wound healing. In the proliferative phase of wound healing, zinc is required for fibroblast replication and collagen synthesis; in the remodeling phase, zinc-dependent metalloproteinases are required for extracellular matrix reorganization. Zinc also plays a key role in immune function by supporting neutrophil chemotaxis, macrophage activity, and T-lymphocyte proliferation — all critical for clearing wound bacteria and initiating healing. This patient has a confirmed low serum zinc level of 52 mcg/dL, likely multifactorial in etiology: her renal diet restricts zinc-rich foods (red meat, shellfish), CKD causes urinary zinc wasting and impaired intestinal absorption, and her overall nutritional status is poor (albumin 2.6, prealbumin 10). The combination of low zinc, hypoalbuminemia, and diabetes (which independently impairs wound healing through reduced growth factor signaling and microvascular disease) creates a profound vulnerability to wound dehiscence. Zinc supplementation has been shown in clinical studies to accelerate wound healing in zinc-deficient patients. Nutritional optimization, including adequate protein and micronutrient repletion, is an essential component of postoperative wound care in high-risk patients.
(Choice E)
Vitamin A deficiency impairing epithelialization and keratinocyte differentiation
Vitamin A deficiency can impair wound healing by disrupting keratinocyte differentiation and re-epithelialization; however, there is no clinical or laboratory evidence of vitamin A deficiency in this patient. Vitamin A deficiency would be suggested by night blindness or xerophthalmia. The documented low zinc level in the setting of chronic kidney disease and a restrictive diet provides a more specific and supported explanation for this patient's wound healing failure.

pages.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks gestation visits the emergency department due to regular, strong uterine contractions that began 6 hours ago, accompanied by a sudden gush of clear fluid from her vagina. She denies any vaginal bleeding and has not attended any prenatal appointments. Upon examination, her vital signs are normal. A sterile speculum exam reveals abundant leaking of fluid, and the cervix is noted to be 5 cm dilated and 90% effaced. Ultrasound imaging conducted in the ER identifies a low amniotic fluid index of 3 along with significant fetal limb deformities and an underdeveloped thoracic cavity. What is the most appropriate management step for this scenario?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This clinical presentation strongly suggests Potter sequence (formerly Potter syndrome) secondary to severe oligohydramnios, likely from bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysplasia. The constellation of findings - severe oligohydramnios (AFI of 3), limb deformities, and underdeveloped thoracic cavity with associated pulmonary hypoplasia - indicates a lethal condition incompatible with extrauterine life. The patient presents with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) at 30 weeks gestation, evidenced by the sudden gush of clear fluid and continued leakage on speculum examination. She is also in active preterm labor with cervical dilation of 5 cm and 90% effacement. In cases of lethal fetal anomalies, standard preterm labor management (corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, tocolytics, expectant management) is not indicated because these interventions cannot alter the ultimate fetal outcome. The primary goal becomes minimizing maternal morbidity. Allowing vaginal delivery to proceed naturally avoids the increased risks associated with cesarean section while providing appropriate comfort care. This approach respects the family's grief process while maintaining the safest course for maternal health.
(Choice A)
Commence maternal corticosteroid therapy
Corticosteroids are given to accelerate fetal lung maturity in viable preterm fetuses. However, with severe pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios and other lethal anomalies present, steroids would not improve outcomes and prolonging pregnancy is not beneficial.
(Choice B)
Proceed with vaginal delivery
Given the fetal anomalies incompatible with life, allowing labor to continue is indicated.
(Choice C)
Explore amnioinfusion with labor-suppressing medication
Amnioinfusion and tocolytics are used to manage oligohydramnios and preterm labor in viable pregnancies. Given the lethal fetal anomalies and poor prognosis, these interventions would unnecessarily prolong pregnancy without benefit while potentially increasing maternal risks.
(Choice D)
Plan an emergency cesarean delivery
Emergency cesarean delivery is not indicated because the fetal anomalies are incompatible with life. C-section carries increased maternal morbidity compared to vaginal delivery without providing any fetal benefit in this case of lethal congenital anomalies.

pages.question: A 14-year-old girl visits the dermatologist due to skin concerns. She reveals light-colored patches on her arms and a growing number of small nodules on her eyes. Her family history notes seizures during early childhood, which have resolved. No ongoing medications are listed. A physical exam identifies several hypomelanotic macules and fleshy, dome-shaped papules on her forehead. Retina examination highlights lesions on both eyes. What potential complication is this patient most susceptible to?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by benign tumor formation in multiple organ systems. Key diagnostic features include hypomelanotic macules (ash leaf spots), facial angiofibromas, and retinal hamartomas. The condition predisposes patients to various tumors including renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, requiring regular monitoring and surveillance.
(Choice A)
Development of early-onset dementia
Early-onset dementia is not a typical feature of tuberous sclerosis complex, though intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorders can occur in some patients.
(Choice B)
Onset of liver insufficiency
Liver insufficiency is not associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. The condition primarily affects the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and lungs.
(Choice C)
Formation of tumors
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is associated with benign tumor formation in multiple organ systems, including renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas.
(Choice D)
Risk of developing hemoptysis
Hemoptysis is not a recognized complication of tuberous sclerosis complex, though pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) can occur and cause pneumothorax rather than bleeding.
(Choice E)
Susceptibility to pancreatitis
Tuberous sclerosis complex does not predispose patients to pancreatitis. The condition primarily affects the skin, brain, kidneys, heart, and lungs.

pages.question: A 44-year-old woman from a rural region of northeastern China presents to a cardiology clinic after being evacuated following a local cluster of unexplained cardiac deaths in her village. She reports progressive exertional dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, and fatigue over the past four months. The region has a known history of selenium-depleted soil. She eats a subsistence diet consisting primarily of locally grown grains and vegetables with minimal animal products. On examination, her blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and she has jugular venous distension, bilateral crackles at the lung bases, and 2+ pitting edema to the knees. Echocardiogram shows four-chamber dilation with an ejection fraction of 22%. Serum selenium level is critically low. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological mechanism by which selenium deficiency causes this patient's cardiac dysfunction?

answers.text:
Selenium deficiency causing mitochondrial complex I dysfunction and impaired ATP synthesis in high-energy-demand cardiac tissue
(25%)

Selenium deficiency causing accumulation of toxic selenium metabolites that directly damage cardiac ion channels
(0%)

Selenium deficiency impairing iodothyronine deiodinase activity, resulting in hypothyroid cardiomyopathy from reduced T3 production
(25%)

Selenium deficiency reducing selenoprotein P expression, impairing cardiomyocyte calcium homeostasis and causing contractile dysfunction
(25%)

Selenium deficiency impairing glutathione peroxidase activity, allowing unchecked reactive oxygen species accumulation and cardiomyocyte oxidative injury
(25%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has Keshan disease, an endemic selenium deficiency cardiomyopathy affecting populations in selenium-depleted regions of China. Selenium is a critical component of glutathione peroxidases that protect cardiomyocytes from oxidative damage. Deficiency allows unchecked reactive oxygen species accumulation, causing cardiomyocyte necrosis and dilated cardiomyopathy.
(Choice A)
Selenium deficiency causing mitochondrial complex I dysfunction and impaired ATP synthesis in high-energy-demand cardiac tissue
While selenium deficiency does cause mitochondrial dysfunction indirectly through oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and enzymes, selenium is not a direct structural component of mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes like complex I. Primary mitochondrial complex I deficiency is a distinct genetic disorder with different clinical features. The mechanism of Keshan disease cardiomyopathy specifically involves loss of selenium-dependent antioxidant protection rather than primary mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction.
(Choice B)
Selenium deficiency causing accumulation of toxic selenium metabolites that directly damage cardiac ion channels
Selenium deficiency is characterized by inadequate selenium, not accumulation of toxic selenium metabolites. Selenium toxicity (selenosis) from excess selenium intake causes hair loss, nail changes, garlic-smelling breath, and neurological symptoms, not cardiomyopathy. Keshan disease results from selenium insufficiency impairing antioxidant defense, not from toxic selenium metabolite accumulation.
(Choice C)
Selenium deficiency impairing iodothyronine deiodinase activity, resulting in hypothyroid cardiomyopathy from reduced T3 production
Selenium is indeed a cofactor for iodothyronine deiodinases that convert T4 to active T3, and selenium deficiency can impair thyroid hormone metabolism. However, hypothyroid cardiomyopathy typically presents with bradycardia, reduced contractility, and diastolic dysfunction rather than the four-chamber dilated cardiomyopathy with tachycardia and systolic dysfunction seen here. The primary mechanism of Keshan disease cardiomyopathy is oxidative cardiomyocyte injury from impaired glutathione peroxidase activity, not thyroid hormone deficiency.
(Choice D)
Selenium deficiency reducing selenoprotein P expression, impairing cardiomyocyte calcium homeostasis and causing contractile dysfunction
Selenoprotein P is the primary selenium transport protein in plasma and is reduced in selenium deficiency. While impaired calcium handling contributes to various cardiomyopathies, the specific mechanism of Keshan disease cardiomyopathy is oxidative injury from glutathione peroxidase deficiency rather than primary selenoprotein P-mediated calcium dysregulation.
(Choice E)
Selenium deficiency impairing glutathione peroxidase activity, allowing unchecked reactive oxygen species accumulation and cardiomyocyte oxidative injury
Selenium is an essential component of selenoproteins, most critically glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and thioredoxin reductase, which are the primary antioxidant defense enzymes in cardiomyocytes. Selenium deficiency severely impairs GPx activity, allowing reactive oxygen species (ROS) including hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides to accumulate unchecked within cardiomyocytes. This oxidative stress causes mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane lipid peroxidation, and ultimately cardiomyocyte necrosis, producing the four-chamber dilated cardiomyopathy of Keshan disease. The disease is endemic to a geographic band of selenium-depleted soil stretching from northeastern to southwestern China. Treatment and prevention involve selenium supplementation, typically as sodium selenite. Selenium-rich foods include Brazil nuts, seafood, organ meats, and grains grown in selenium-replete soil.

pages.question: A 10-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with persistent fever and worsening shortness of breath. Three days ago, she was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia based on clinical symptoms and a chest x-ray showing left lower lobe consolidation; she was started on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Despite treatment, her symptoms have not improved, and she now reports chest pain on the left side. Examination reveals temperature of 38.8°C (101.8°F), respiratory rate of 35 breaths per minute, heart rate of 115 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. Lung auscultation shows decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the left lower lung field. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Continue current antibiotic therapy and reassess in 24 hours
(1.33%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient with pneumonia has persistent fever and worsening respiratory symptoms despite 72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy, along with physical findings suggestive of a parapneumonic effusion (decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion). A repeat chest x-ray is indicated to evaluate for complications such as pleural effusion.
(Choice A)
Perform immediate thoracentesis
Thoracentesis is premature without confirmatory imaging. While the physical findings suggest parapneumonic effusion, chest x-ray must first confirm the presence and size of effusion before proceeding to drainage, which is typically reserved for moderate to large effusions or those causing significant respiratory compromise.
(Choice B)
Obtain a repeat chest x-ray
A repeat chest x-ray is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for pneumonia complications such as parapneumonic effusion in a child not improving after 48-72 hours of therapy.
(Choice C)
Order a chest CT scan
While chest CT provides detailed imaging, it is not the initial imaging modality for suspected parapneumonic effusion. Chest x-ray is the appropriate first-line imaging study - less invasive, lower radiation exposure, and adequate for detecting and assessing pleural effusions in pediatric patients.
(Choice D)
Switch to oral azithromycin
Switching to azithromycin without imaging evaluation is inappropriate because the patient's clinical deterioration and physical findings (decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion) suggest possible parapneumonic effusion rather than antibiotic resistance or atypical pathogen coverage needs.
(Choice E)
Continue current antibiotic therapy and reassess in 24 hours
Continuing the current therapy without further evaluation is inappropriate given the lack of improvement after 72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy, new chest pain, and physical findings suggestive of complications (decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion).

pages.question:
A 42-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit after developing acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) secondary to severe viral pneumonia. She is intubated and mechanically ventilated with the following settings: FiO2 0.8, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) 8 cm H2O, tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Lab values and a chest x-ray are shown below. Despite these settings, her oxygenation remains poor. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to improve her oxygenation?



White blood cell count	8200/mm3
Neutrophils	65%
Lymphocytes	25%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Red blood cell count	4.6x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	41%
Platelet count	260000/µL
Arterial pH	7.32
PaCO2	48 mm Hg
PaO2	55 mm Hg
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	24 mEq/L

answers.text:
Increase respiratory rate to 30 breaths/min to improve ventilation
(4.11%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has ARDS secondary to viral pneumonia with persistent hypoxemia despite high FiO2. Increasing PEEP is the most appropriate step as it recruits collapsed alveoli, reduces intrapulmonary shunting, and allows for potential reduction in FiO2 to minimize oxygen toxicity. Increasing FiO2 further risks oxygen toxicity without addressing alveolar collapse. Increasing tidal volume could cause volutrauma in ARDS. Increasing respiratory rate may not directly improve oxygenation and could exacerbate air trapping. Administering inhaled nitric oxide is not first-line and lacks strong evidence for routine use in ARDS.
(Choice A)
Increase tidal volume to 8 mL/kg
Increasing tidal volume contradicts lung-protective ventilation strategies in ARDS, which recommend low tidal volumes (4-8 mL/kg, ideally 6 mL/kg) to prevent volutrauma.
(Choice B)
Administer inhaled nitric oxide
Inhaled nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator that can improve ventilation-perfusion matching in some ARDS patients, but it is not a first-line intervention. Studies have not shown mortality benefit, and it should be reserved for severe, refractory hypoxemia after optimizing conventional ventilator settings including PEEP. It is also expensive and requires specialized monitoring.
(Choice C)
Increase respiratory rate to 30 breaths/min to improve ventilation
Increasing respiratory rate primarily affects ventilation and CO2 removal rather than oxygenation. The patient's CO2 is only mildly elevated (48 mmHg), and increasing respiratory rate will not address the fundamental problem of impaired gas exchange due to alveolar collapse. Higher respiratory rates may also lead to auto-PEEP, air trapping, and increased risk of barotrauma.
(Choice D)
Increase FiO2 to 1.0
Increasing FiO2 to 1.0 may temporarily improve PaO2 but does not address the underlying problem of alveolar collapse and intrapulmonary shunting in ARDS. Additionally, prolonged exposure to high FiO2 (>0.6) increases the risk of oxygen toxicity and should be avoided when possible.
(Choice E)
Increase positive end-expiratory pressure
Increasing PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli, improves oxygenation by reducing shunting, and is a key strategy in ARDS management to allow FiO2 reduction.

pages.question: A 72-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was recently started on sacubitril-valsartan for symptom management. He has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. This morning, he notices swelling of his tongue and lips, along with mild difficulty swallowing. He denies any new foods, insect bites, or other medications. Vital signs taken at home are stable. What is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

answers.text:
Schedule an urgent outpatient clinic visit within the next 24 hours
(0%)

Go to the emergency department immediately
(90.91%)

Discontinue sacubitril-valsartan and start lisinopril instead
(5.68%)

Increase the dose of his loop diuretic and follow up in one week
(0%)

Take an over-the-counter antihistamine and monitor symptoms at home
(3.41%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's tongue and lip swelling with difficulty swallowing is indicative of angioedema, an adverse effect associated with sacubitril-valsartan due to its neprilysin inhibition increasing bradykinin levels. This condition can rapidly progress to airway compromise, necessitating immediate emergency department evaluation. Options like taking an antihistamine, scheduling a clinic visit, adjusting medications at home, or monitoring symptoms are inadequate and could delay critical intervention.
(Choice A)
Schedule an urgent outpatient clinic visit within the next 24 hours
Delaying evaluation for potential angioedema risks airway compromise; immediate assessment is necessary.
(Choice B)
Go to the emergency department immediately
Angioedema from sacubitril-valsartan can escalate quickly to airway obstruction, requiring urgent medical evaluation and possible interventions like intubation or epinephrine.
(Choice C)
Discontinue sacubitril-valsartan and start lisinopril instead
ACE inhibitors like lisinopril also increase bradykinin levels and could potentially worsen angioedema. Additionally, medication changes do not address the current acute presentation requiring immediate evaluation for potential airway compromise.
(Choice D)
Increase the dose of his loop diuretic and follow up in one week
The patient's symptoms represent angioedema, not heart failure exacerbation. Increasing diuretics would not address the underlying bradykinin-mediated swelling and ignores the potential for rapid progression to airway obstruction.
(Choice E)
Take an over-the-counter antihistamine and monitor symptoms at home
While antihistamines may help with histamine-mediated allergic reactions, angioedema from sacubitril-valsartan involves bradykinin-mediated pathways that do not respond to antihistamines. This condition can progress rapidly to life-threatening airway obstruction.

pages.question: A 15-year-old African American female presents to the clinic with concerns over primary amenorrhea. She recalls an episode of high-grade fever and hospitalization due to pneumonia at age 8. On examination, she shows the presence of minimal facial and body hair. Muscle development is consistent with female norms. Palpation reveals an inguinal mass. A karyotype reveals 46, XY. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This case illustrates complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS), where patients have a 46,XY karyotype but develop female external genitalia due to defective androgen receptors. The inguinal masses represent undescended testes. Breast development occurs due to peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens, while the absence of pubic and facial hair confirms androgen resistance. The undescended testes carry a 25-50% malignancy risk, making gonadectomy the immediate priority, typically performed after pubertal development is complete. Post-gonadectomy, patients require estrogen replacement therapy and comprehensive counseling regarding the condition, fertility implications, and psychosocial support.
(Choice A)
Initiate high-dose testosterone therapy
Testosterone therapy is contraindicated because the androgen receptors are defective in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, making tissues unresponsive to androgens. This would not improve virilization and could potentially increase estrogen levels through peripheral conversion.
(Choice B)
Refer for genetic counseling only
While genetic counseling is important for understanding the condition and family planning implications, it does not address the immediate medical priority of preventing testicular malignancy. Gonadectomy should be performed first, followed by genetic counseling.
(Choice C)
Arrange for gonadectomy
This is the correct management strategy to prevent testicular carcinoma risk associated with undescended testes in individuals with androgen insensitivity.
(Choice D)
Schedule exploratory laparoscopy
While laparoscopy could locate the undescended testes, it delays definitive management. The priority is gonadectomy to prevent malignant transformation, which has a 25-50% risk in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome if gonads are not removed.
(Choice E)
Vitamin D supplementation
Vitamin D supplementation addresses bone health but is irrelevant to the primary concern of malignancy risk from undescended testes in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome.

pages.question: A 55-year-old female presents with generalized fatigue, itching, and dark urine for the past week. She denies any abdominal pain, hematemesis, or changes in bowel habits. Her vital signs are stable. On physical examination, her sclerae are icteric, and the abdominal examination reveals mild hepatomegaly without tenderness or masses. Laboratory findings show total bilirubin of 12.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 9.8 mg/dL, AST of 35 IU/L, ALT of 38 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase of 950 IU/L, and serum albumin of 4.0 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient exhibits symptoms indicative of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. This suggests the possibility of biliary obstruction, either from intrahepatic or extrahepatic origin. An ultrasound of the abdomen is a non-invasive test that helps rule out an anatomical cause such as gallstones or a mass causing compression, making it the first-line investigation in this scenario.
(Choice A)
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography
MRCP provides excellent visualization of the biliary and pancreatic ducts but is typically reserved as a second-line imaging modality after ultrasound. It is more expensive and time-consuming than ultrasound, making it inappropriate as the initial imaging study.
(Choice B)
Abdominal ultrasound
This non-invasive imaging modality helps determine if there's an obstruction in the biliary tree, which is crucial for patients with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
(Choice C)
Liver biopsy
Not the immediate next step; liver biopsy is more invasive and used for assessing liver architecture or diagnosing certain liver diseases.
(Choice D)
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
Ferritin and transferrin saturation evaluate for hemochromatosis, which typically causes hepatocellular injury with elevated transaminases. This patient's cholestatic pattern (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal AST/ALT) suggests biliary pathology rather than iron overload.
(Choice E)
Serum ceruloplasmin level
Ceruloplasmin level is used to evaluate for Wilson's disease, which typically presents with hepatocellular injury (elevated AST/ALT) rather than the cholestatic pattern (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal transaminases) seen in this patient.

pages.question: A 52-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, and recent episodes of uncontrolled vomiting is brought to the emergency department. He reports feeling lightheaded and dizzy over the past few days. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F), heart rate of 88/min, respiratory rate of 12/min, and blood pressure of 95/64 mmHg when supine. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. Laboratory tests show: Blood pH 7.47, PaO2 101 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L, Sodium 137 mEq/L, Potassium 2.8 mEq/L, Chloride 96 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to address the patient's acid-base disturbance?

answers.text:
Intravenous normal saline and potassium chloride
(88.51%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Contraction alkalosis from prolonged vomiting results from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and volume depletion. The volume loss activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to continued hydrogen ion loss and potassium wasting by the kidneys, perpetuating alkalosis and hypokalemia. Treatment requires simultaneous correction of volume depletion with normal saline (to interrupt RAAS activation) and potassium chloride replacement (to correct hypokalemia and provide chloride for bicarbonate excretion). This dual approach addresses both the underlying pathophysiology and the electrolyte abnormalities.
(Choice A)
Oral sodium chloride supplements
While oral sodium chloride could theoretically help, this patient shows signs of significant volume depletion (hypotension, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor) requiring immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation. Oral supplementation would be inadequate for the acute correction needed and may be poorly tolerated given the recent vomiting history.
(Choice B)
Intravenous potassium chloride alone
While hypokalemia correction is essential, potassium chloride alone will not address the volume depletion that drives contraction alkalosis. Without volume restoration with normal saline, the kidneys continue activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, perpetuating hydrogen ion loss and alkalosis despite potassium repletion.
(Choice C)
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated in metabolic alkalosis as it would worsen the existing alkalemia (pH 7.47) and elevated bicarbonate (30 mEq/L). This patient needs interventions to normalize pH by addressing the underlying volume depletion and electrolyte losses, not further alkalinization.
(Choice D)
Intravenous dextrose solution
Dextrose solution does not contain the sodium and chloride needed to restore extracellular volume or the potassium chloride needed to correct hypokalemia. In contraction alkalosis, specific electrolyte replacement with normal saline and potassium chloride is required to interrupt the pathophysiologic cycle of volume depletion and continued alkali retention.
(Choice E)
Intravenous normal saline and potassium chloride
Correct choice. Administering normal saline will restore extracellular fluid volume, and potassium chloride will correct hypokalemia, effectively treating contraction alkalosis.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman at 10 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with severe nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake for the past 10 days. She has lost 8 kg and appears dehydrated. On examination, she is confused, exhibits horizontal nystagmus, and has an unsteady gait. Her blood glucose level is 65 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic intervention?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with hyperemesis gravidarum leading to severe malnutrition and thiamine deficiency, manifesting as Wernicke encephalopathy. The classic triad includes altered mental status (confusion), ocular dysfunction (horizontal nystagmus), and cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia). Immediate empirical thiamine administration is critical and must precede or accompany glucose administration to prevent further neurological deterioration. While supportive care including IV fluids and antiemetics may be needed, they do not address the life-threatening thiamine deficiency.
(Choice A)
Ondansetron
While this dehydrated patient requires IV fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replacement as part of comprehensive care, this intervention does not address the acute neurological emergency of thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy. The triad of confusion, nystagmus, and ataxia requires immediate thiamine replacement.
(Choice B)
Folic acid
Folic acid supplementation is important during pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects, but it does not treat thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. The patient's neurological symptoms represent Wernicke encephalopathy, which specifically results from thiamine deficiency and requires thiamine replacement.
(Choice C)
Thiamine
Thiamine is the correct initial treatment for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency in this malnourished patient.
(Choice D)
Intravenous fluids with electrolytes
Rehydration is important but does not treat the underlying thiamine deficiency responsible for the encephalopathy, nystagmus, and ataxia.
(Choice E)
Intravenous glucose
While this patient has hypoglycemia that requires correction, administering intravenous glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy by rapidly depleting the remaining thiamine stores needed for glucose metabolism. Thiamine must be given first or concurrently with glucose.

pages.question: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of Crohn's disease presents to clinic with a 3-month history of painful cracks at the corners of her mouth, a red, swollen tongue, and irritated, watery eyes with sensitivity to light. She has been on long-term sulfasalazine therapy and reports poor appetite due to chronic abdominal pain. On examination, she has angular cheilitis, magenta discoloration of the tongue, and slit-lamp evaluation reveals superficial corneal vascularization extending from the limbus. Her hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL with a normochromic normocytic pattern. Which of the following nutritional deficiencies best explains this patient's constellation of findings?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency classically presents with the triad of angular cheilitis, glossitis with magenta tongue discoloration, and corneal vascularization (interstitial keratitis). It is particularly common in malabsorption syndromes such as Crohn's disease and in patients on sulfasalazine, which impairs riboflavin absorption. Recognition of this specific triad helps distinguish riboflavin deficiency from other B-vitamin deficiencies that may co-occur in these clinical contexts.
(Choice A)
Riboflavin deficiency
Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is essential for oxidative metabolism as a precursor to FAD and FMN coenzymes. Its deficiency characteristically produces the triad of angular cheilitis (painful fissures at the oral commissures), glossitis with a magenta or purplish tongue discoloration, and corneal vascularization extending from the limbus — a finding nearly pathognomonic for riboflavin deficiency. Crohn's disease impairs riboflavin absorption in the small intestine, and sulfasalazine further inhibits riboflavin transport, making this patient doubly at risk. The normochromic normocytic anemia can also result from riboflavin deficiency, which impairs erythroid maturation. Treatment involves oral riboflavin supplementation, and patients with malabsorption may require parenteral repletion in severe cases. Co-occurring B-vitamin deficiencies are common in this setting and should also be assessed.
(Choice B)
Vitamin A deficiency
Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia with progressive stages: night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis, and potentially keratomalacia. However, it does not cause the superficial corneal vascularization extending from the limbus that is pathognomonic for riboflavin deficiency. The oral manifestations (angular cheilitis, magenta tongue) are also not characteristic of vitamin A deficiency.
(Choice C)
Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency primarily causes megaloblastic anemia with macrocytic red blood cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. While glossitis can occur with folate deficiency, it typically presents as a smooth, beefy-red tongue rather than the magenta discoloration seen here. The angular cheilitis and corneal vascularization are not features of folate deficiency, and the normocytic anemia makes folate deficiency unlikely.
(Choice D)
Pyridoxine deficiency
Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause angular cheilitis and glossitis, but these findings overlap with many B-vitamin deficiencies. The key distinguishing feature is that B6 deficiency does not cause corneal vascularization, which is nearly pathognomonic for riboflavin deficiency. Additionally, B6 deficiency characteristically produces peripheral sensory neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia (microcytic with increased iron stores), neither of which is present in this case.
(Choice E)
Niacin deficiency
Niacin deficiency causes pellagra with the classic '4 Ds': dermatitis (symmetric photosensitive rash in sun-exposed areas), diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated. The dermatitis is the most prominent feature, appearing as a symmetric, hyperpigmented rash on sun-exposed areas. Angular cheilitis and corneal vascularization are not characteristic of pellagra, making this diagnosis inconsistent with the patient's presentation.

pages.question: A 27-year-old woman had just given birth to a full-term baby girl. On examination, the infant presents with small body weight, microcephaly, hypoplasia of the distal phalanges of fingers and toes, increased body hair, and a cleft palate. The birth weight was recorded at 2.6kg (5.7lbs). What might further evaluation of the mother's history reveal as a likely cause?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Carbamazepine and other anticonvulsants can cause distinct teratogenic syndromes during pregnancy. Recognition of these characteristic patterns of dysmorphic features is essential for counseling patients with epilepsy about medication risks and benefits during pregnancy.
(Choice A)
Malnourishment during pregnancy
Malnourishment during pregnancy typically causes symmetric growth restriction and low birth weight, but does not produce the specific constellation of dysmorphic features described (microcephaly, cleft palate, digital hypoplasia, hirsutism).
(Choice B)
Lisinopril use during pregnancy
ACE inhibitors like lisinopril cause fetopathy primarily in the second and third trimesters, resulting in oligohydramnios, renal dysgenesis, growth restriction, and limb contractures. The facial dysmorphism and digital anomalies described are not typical of ACE inhibitor fetopathy.
(Choice C)
Gestational diabetes
Gestational diabetes can lead to macrosomia or large for gestational age babies, not the features described in this case.
(Choice D)
Valproate use
Valproate teratogenicity primarily causes neural tube defects (spina bifida), cognitive impairment, and distinctive facial features. However, the specific pattern of distal digital hypoplasia and hirsutism described here is more characteristic of anticonvulsants like carbamazepine.
(Choice E)
Carbamazepine use
Carbamazepine causes a distinct teratogenic syndrome characterized by microcephaly, developmental delays, facial dysmorphism (including cleft palate), nail hypoplasia, and growth retardation. While similar to fetal hydantoin syndrome, it is not the same condition.

pages.question: A 58-year-old woman with a 40-pack-year smoking history and long-term exposure to bird droppings as a pigeon breeder presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, chronic cough, and occasional wheezing. She notes increasing difficulty climbing stairs and performing household chores. Physical examination reveals a thin build, increased anteroposterior chest diameter, hyperresonance on percussion, and prolonged expiratory phase. Pulmonary function tests demonstrate a FEV1 of 50% predicted, FVC of 75% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55, total lung capacity (TLC) of 140% predicted, and residual volume (RV) of 160% predicted. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the decreased vital capacity and increased total lung capacity in this patient?

answers.text:
Reduced elastic recoil of the lungs
(26.32%)

Excessive mucus production and airway inflammation
(3.95%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), likely with both emphysema and chronic bronchitis components. While her bird exposure history raises concern for concurrent hypersensitivity pneumonitis, the obstructive pattern on pulmonary function tests (FEV1/FVC <0.7, increased TLC and RV) indicates COPD pathophysiology predominates. The primary mechanism causing decreased vital capacity and increased total lung capacity is air trapping due to expiratory airflow limitation, which prevents complete lung emptying and leads to hyperinflation.
(Choice A)
Reduced elastic recoil of the lungs
While reduced elastic recoil is a key pathophysiologic feature of emphysema that contributes to expiratory airflow limitation, air trapping is the direct mechanism that causes the specific lung volume changes described (increased RV, increased TLC, decreased VC). Reduced elastic recoil enables air trapping but is not itself the mechanism of volume change.
(Choice B)
Excessive mucus production and airway inflammation
While inflammation and fibrosis of alveoli occur in hypersensitivity pneumonitis (which this patient may have from bird exposure), these changes typically cause restrictive lung disease with decreased TLC and VC. The obstructive pattern with increased TLC seen here indicates that COPD pathophysiology predominates, where air trapping rather than fibrosis is the primary mechanism.
(Choice C)
Air trapping during expiration
Air trapping due to expiratory airflow limitation is the primary mechanism in COPD that leads to increased residual volume, hyperinflation (increased TLC), and consequently decreased vital capacity, as the lungs cannot fully empty.
(Choice D)
Inflammation and fibrosis of alveoli
Alveolar inflammation and fibrosis are more characteristic of interstitial lung diseases like hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which can cause restrictive patterns with decreased TLC, not the obstructive pattern with increased TLC seen here.
(Choice E)
Increased pulmonary vascular pressure
Pulmonary hypertension can develop in advanced COPD due to hypoxic vasoconstriction, but it does not directly cause air trapping or the observed changes in lung volumes.

pages.question: A large urban hospital system is transitioning to an accountable care organization model to manage care for patients with type 2 diabetes. The administration aims to incentivize providers to focus on preventive measures and efficient resource allocation. Which of the following strategies best aligns with a pay-for-performance program in this context?

answers.text:
Restricting endocrinology referrals unless patients have HbA1c >9% or diabetic complications
(10.19%)

Providing bonuses to endocrinologists based on the percentage of their patients who achieve glycemic control targets and complete annual foot exams
(77.78%)

Requiring prior authorization for all diabetes medications including insulin and metformin to control costs
(0.93%)

Implementing a flat fee for all diabetes-related consultations regardless of outcomes
(11.11%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Pay-for-performance (P4P) programs in accountable care organizations link financial incentives to predefined quality metrics such as HbA1c targets, preventive screening completion rates, and patient satisfaction scores. These programs optimize resource use by rewarding evidence-based care and appropriate utilization rather than restricting access. Unlike traditional cost-containment strategies that may delay or limit care, P4P aligns provider incentives with improved patient outcomes and efficient resource allocation.
(Choice A)
Restricting endocrinology referrals unless patients have HbA1c >9% or diabetic complications
